---
title: "Filling Raster Gaps with Cokriging"
date: 2026-09-20
categories: [tool, geostatistics]
description: "A cloud-covered satellite band, a sparse survey rasterized with mostly-empty cells: fill the gaps using a second, correlated band as a covariate, via cokriging instead of single-variable kriging. Runs on R; Python shown as reference only."
---

The [kriging article](/posts/kriging-soil-sampling.html) on this site
predicts a value everywhere from scattered points, using only how far
apart those points are. But a raster with gaps is a different problem:
you already have a dense grid, most of it valid, and a second band of
the *same file* that's correlated with it and valid where it isn't,
at least in part (elevation next to a cloud-gapped spectral band,
say).
Ignoring that second band and kriging the gaps from the target's own
neighbours alone throws away real information. Cokriging is kriging
that uses it: fit a model of how the *two* bands vary together, not
just how one varies with distance, then predict the missing values
from wherever the covariate is available.

Prefer to skip straight to a result? The
[standalone tool](/tools/raster-gap-filler.html) runs the same
computation: upload your own multi-band raster, pick the two bands,
and it fills the gaps for you.

## 1. Upload your raster

A multi-band GeoTIFF (`.tif`/`.tiff`) with at least two bands: one you
want filled (has real gaps, NoData cells), one that doesn't. That
second band is the covariate: elevation, another spectral band,
anything correlated with the first.

::: {#lab-upload}
:::

## 2. Why a covariate band helps

If you've read the [kriging article](/posts/kriging-soil-sampling.html),
you've already met the variogram: bin every pair of points by
distance, average their squared difference within each bin (half of
it, actually, which is why the axis says semivariance, not variance),
fit a smooth curve to those bins. That curve's nugget, sill, and range
describe how one variable varies with itself over distance. Cokriging
needs one more piece: the **cross-variogram**, the same idea applied to
*two* variables at once. It asks how much the target's value at one
location tends to differ from the covariate's value at *another*
location, as a function of the distance between them.

Fitting a target's variogram, a covariate's variogram, and their
cross-variogram together, consistently enough that the combined system
stays mathematically valid (technically: positive definite), is a
**linear model of coregionalization** (LMC). Once fit, predicting the
target at a gap uses both: the target's own nearby known values, *and*
the covariate's value right there, weighted by how strongly the two
actually move together. Where the covariate is missing too, there's
nothing extra to weight in. Cokriging can't fill that pixel any
differently than plain kriging could, which is why this article (and
the standalone tool) leaves those cells empty rather than guessing.

## R — runnable in this browser

```{.webgeods-r #cokriging-fit-r}
#| package: terra, sf, sp, gstat, jsonlite
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(gstat)

r <- tryCatch(rast("/uploaded.tif"), error = function(e) NULL)

if (is.null(r)) {
  # Same synthetic 2-band raster the standalone tool's own example
  # uses: a Gaussian-hill trend, a covariate that's a scaled, shifted,
  # independently-noised version of the SAME trend (real correlation,
  # not a copy), and two DIFFERENT gaps -- the target's is bigger, the
  # covariate's is smaller and only partly inside it. That last detail
  # matters: it's what makes "some pixels stay empty" a real,
  # observable outcome below, not a hypothetical.
  set.seed(42)
  n <- 25
  xs <- 0:(n - 1)
  ys <- 0:(n - 1)
  trend <- outer(ys, xs, function(y, x) 100 + 40 * exp(-((x - 12)^2 + (y - 12)^2) / 40))
  target_m <- trend + matrix(rnorm(n * n, sd = 1.5), nrow = n)
  covariate_m <- 0.6 * trend + 20 + matrix(rnorm(n * n, sd = 2), nrow = n)
  target_m[9:17, 9:17] <- NA
  covariate_m[12:14, 12:14] <- NA
  band_target <- rast(target_m, crs = "EPSG:4326")
  band_covariate <- rast(covariate_m, crs = "EPSG:4326")
  ext(band_target) <- c(12.40, 12.40 + n * 0.004, 41.90, 41.90 + n * 0.004)
  ext(band_covariate) <- ext(band_target)
  names(band_target) <- "target"
  names(band_covariate) <- "covariate"
  r <- c(band_target, band_covariate)
  target_i <- 1
  covariate_i <- 2
} else {
  # No band picker in this article (that lives in the standalone
  # tool) -- uses band 1 as the target, band 2 as the covariate.
  if (nlyr(r) < 2) {
    stop("Need a raster with at least 2 bands -- this file only has 1.")
  }
  target_i <- 1
  covariate_i <- 2
}

# The terra -> sp bridge: gstat's own variogram()/krige()/fit.lmc()
# take sp point objects (coordinates(df) <- ~x+y), not a terra
# SpatRaster -- terra doesn't provide that replacement function
# itself. Cell centers and per-band values, aligned by row, in the
# file's OWN crs -- no reprojection, unlike the point-survey case in
# the kriging article: a raster's pixels already sit on a grid with a
# real resolution, not raw lon/lat survey coordinates that need a
# working CRS before distance means anything.
cell_xy <- crds(r, na.rm = FALSE)
df <- data.frame(
  x = cell_xy[, 1], y = cell_xy[, 2],
  target = as.numeric(values(r[[target_i]])),
  covariate = as.numeric(values(r[[covariate_i]]))
)

# Two disjoint pixel sets: data_fit (BOTH bands valid -- fitting only)
# and data_pred (covariate valid, regardless of target -- this is
# where prediction happens in the next cell). data_pred must contain
# data_fit's own locations too, for the cokriging system's local
# context at prediction time -- it does automatically here, since
# data_fit already requires covariate valid, a strict subset of
# data_pred's own condition. Narrowing data_pred to just the target's
# own gaps instead would silently break that.
data_fit <- df[!is.na(df$target) & !is.na(df$covariate), ]
data_pred <- df[!is.na(df$covariate), ]

if (nrow(data_fit) < 5) {
  stop(paste0("Need at least 5 pixels where both bands are valid to fit a coregionalization model -- found ", nrow(data_fit), "."))
}

fit_pts <- data_fit
coordinates(fit_pts) <- ~x + y

# The target's own EMPIRICAL variogram -- method-independent (just
# binned squared differences), so this is computed once here and reused
# below both for the joint fit's own initial guess and for the chart's
# scatter points.
v_emp <- variogram(target ~ 1, fit_pts)
init_psill <- var(data_fit$target)

# Both variables registered on the SAME point object (fit_pts, same
# rows, same order) -- registering them on mismatched location sets
# instead forces gstat to compute a genuine zero-distance bin between
# the two variables' own locations, which fit.method=7 (Cressie's
# weights, gstat's own default) divides by. correct.diagonal fixes a
# separate, related near-singular-matrix issue found the same way.
v_cross <- variogram(gstat(gstat(NULL, id = "target", formula = target ~ 1, data = fit_pts), id = "covariate", formula = covariate ~ 1, data = fit_pts))

# fit.lmc()'s optimizer is LOCAL, not global, and a single starting
# range is a real gamble for a joint fit: passing it the classic
# single-variable rule of thumb (max distance / 3) trapped it in a
# clearly worse solution on this exact data -- confirmed live, trying
# several starting ranges: sum-of-squared-error against the target's
# own empirical points ranged from 1878 (at max/3) down to 173 (at the
# FULL max distance), roughly a 10x difference, with the fitted sill
# and range moving enough to visibly change the chart below, not just
# the decimals. So instead of committing to one guess, this tries a
# small spread of them and keeps whichever lands closest to the
# target's own empirical variogram -- the same fit.method=7-then-1
# fallback runs for each one (Cressie's weights first, N-only weights
# only if that specific starting point makes them singular).
sse_against_target <- function(model_df) {
  vl <- variogramLine(model_df, dist_vector = v_emp$dist)
  sum((v_emp$gamma - vl$gamma)^2)
}
fit_lmc_candidate <- function(init_range) {
  lmc_model <- vgm(psill = init_psill, model = "Sph", range = init_range, nugget = init_psill / 4)
  fresh_g <- function() gstat(gstat(NULL, id = "target", formula = target ~ 1, data = fit_pts), id = "covariate", formula = covariate ~ 1, data = fit_pts)
  gf <- tryCatch(fit.lmc(v_cross, fresh_g(), model = lmc_model, fit.method = 7, correct.diagonal = 1.01), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(gf)) gf <- tryCatch(fit.lmc(v_cross, fresh_g(), model = lmc_model, fit.method = 1, correct.diagonal = 1.01), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(gf)) return(NULL)
  list(g_fit = gf, sse = sse_against_target(gf$model[["target"]]))
}

candidates <- Filter(Negate(is.null), lapply(max(v_cross$dist) * c(1 / 6, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1), fit_lmc_candidate))
if (length(candidates) == 0) {
  stop("Could not fit a coregionalization model between these two bands -- often too few co-located pixels, or the bands aren't actually correlated.")
}
g_fit <- candidates[[which.min(sapply(candidates, function(c) c$sse))]]$g_fit

# nugget/partialSill/range AND the chart's fitted curve both come from
# the TARGET's own component of this joint fit -- not a separately-fit
# standalone variogram. The two can differ noticeably (fit.lmc() must
# satisfy one shared range across target, covariate AND their cross-
# variogram at once, a real constraint a lone fit.variogram() on target
# doesn't have), so showing the standalone version here would draw a
# curve that isn't actually the one cokriging below uses.
target_model <- g_fit$model[["target"]]
nugget_val <- target_model$psill[1]
partial_sill_val <- target_model$psill[2]
range_val <- target_model$range[2]
sample_mean <- mean(data_fit$target)
sample_variance <- var(data_fit$target)
v_line <- variogramLine(target_model, maxdist = max(v_emp$dist), n = 100)

# The raw target band, gaps and all, base64-encoded the same way the
# filled result will be in the next cell -- lets the map below show
# the actual PROBLEM (band 1, real hole visible) before showing the
# fix.
raw_target <- as.numeric(values(r[[target_i]]))
con <- rawConnection(raw(0), "wb")
writeBin(raw_target, con, size = 4, endian = "little")
raw_bytes <- rawConnectionValue(con)
close(con)
raw_b64 <- jsonlite::base64_enc(raw_bytes)

to_minx_miny_maxx_maxy <- function(spat_extent) {
  b <- as.vector(spat_extent)
  c(as.numeric(b["xmin"]), as.numeric(b["ymin"]), as.numeric(b["xmax"]), as.numeric(b["ymax"]))
}
wgs84_bounds <- tryCatch({
  poly_wgs84 <- project(as.polygons(ext(r), crs = crs(r)), "EPSG:4326")
  to_minx_miny_maxx_maxy(ext(poly_wgs84))
}, error = function(e) to_minx_miny_maxx_maxy(ext(r)))

valid_raw <- raw_target[!is.na(raw_target)]

result_out <- list(
  summary = list(
    targetBand = jsonlite::unbox(target_i),
    covariateBand = jsonlite::unbox(covariate_i),
    coFitPixels = jsonlite::unbox(nrow(data_fit)),
    nugget = jsonlite::unbox(round(nugget_val, 4)),
    partialSill = jsonlite::unbox(round(partial_sill_val, 4)),
    range = jsonlite::unbox(round(range_val, 3)),
    sampleMean = jsonlite::unbox(round(sample_mean, 4)),
    sampleVariance = jsonlite::unbox(round(sample_variance, 4))
  ),
  # dist rounded to 6dp, not 2 -- this raster's own coordinates are
  # degree-scale (a range around 0.01-0.05), so 2dp collapsed most of
  # variogramLine()'s 100 points onto a handful of duplicate x values
  # while gamma kept rising between them -- found live: a fitted
  # "curve" that plotted as a staircase (flat runs and vertical jumps)
  # instead of the smooth line it's supposed to be.
  variogram = list(
    empirical = list(dist = round(v_emp$dist, 6), gamma = round(v_emp$gamma, 5), npairs = v_emp$np),
    fitted = list(dist = round(v_line$dist, 6), gamma = round(v_line$gamma, 5))
  ),
  raster = list(
    width = jsonlite::unbox(ncol(r)),
    height = jsonlite::unbox(nrow(r)),
    data = jsonlite::unbox(raw_b64),
    wgs84Bounds = round(wgs84_bounds, 6),
    min = jsonlite::unbox(round(min(valid_raw), 4)),
    max = jsonlite::unbox(round(max(valid_raw), 4))
  )
)

# r, df, data_fit, data_pred, g_fit and target_i stay in this R
# session's global environment after this cell finishes -- the next
# cell reuses them directly instead of re-reading the file and
# re-fitting, same cross-cell reuse the kriging article's own two
# cells already rely on.
jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result_out, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

# Reference only -- not executable in this browser tool, and NOT a

# assumes the covariate is known at every point you're predicting

## 5. The target's own variogram

This is the target band's direct variogram, the same shape as the
[kriging article's](/posts/kriging-soil-sampling.html) own chart: half
the average squared difference within each distance bin, with the
fitted curve's nugget, sill, and range marked on it. It's not the whole
story. The actual cokriging fit above also needs the covariate's own
variogram and the cross-variogram between the two, neither shown
separately here. But it's the piece that carries over directly from
ordinary kriging, and the one place this article's chart can show
something the reader already knows how to read.

::: {#lab-variogram}
:::

Once the model above looks right, predict the gaps themselves:

::: {.panel-tabset}

## R — runnable in this browser

```{.webgeods-r #cokriging-predict-r}
#| package: terra, sf, sp, gstat, jsonlite
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(sp)
library(gstat)

if (!exists("g_fit") || !exists("data_pred") || !exists("data_fit")) {
  stop("Run the cell in section 4 first -- this step needs its fitted model.")
}

pred_pts <- data_pred
coordinates(pred_pts) <- ~x + y

# Target on its own known locations (fit_pts, reused from the cell
# above), covariate on ALL of data_pred -- then attach the
# already-fitted model as a SEPARATE step. Passing model= directly
# into this gstat() call throws "argument 'formula' is missing" (it
# reads it as a brand-new variable, not the existing fit); this plain
# assignment after the fact is the version that actually works.
g_pred <- gstat(NULL, id = "target", formula = target ~ 1, data = fit_pts)
g_pred <- gstat(g_pred, id = "covariate", formula = covariate ~ 1, data = pred_pts)
g_pred$model <- g_fit$model

k <- predict(g_pred, newdata = pred_pts, nmax = 24, debug.level = 0)

filled <- df$target
pred_index <- which(!is.na(df$covariate))
cokriged <- is.na(df$target[pred_index])
filled[pred_index[cokriged]] <- as.numeric(k$target.pred[cokriged])

n_filled <- sum(cokriged & !is.na(filled[pred_index]))
n_still_na <- sum(is.na(filled))

# Cross-validation on the FIT data -- same gstat.cv() diagnostic used
# on the standalone tool. Its residual column is just "residual", not
# "target.residual" -- found empirically (a multivariate gstat.cv()
# result names target.pred/target.var with the id prefix, but
# residual/observed/zscore/fold without it).
# Fixed seed: the folds are random, so the RMSE would otherwise
# change a little on every run.
set.seed(1)
cv <- tryCatch(gstat.cv(g_fit, nfold = 5, verbose = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
rmse <- if (!is.null(cv)) sqrt(mean(cv$residual^2, na.rm = TRUE)) else NA

filled_valid <- filled[!is.na(filled)]

result_out <- list(
  summary = list(
    pixelsFilled = jsonlite::unbox(n_filled),
    pixelsStillEmpty = jsonlite::unbox(n_still_na),
    crossValidationRmse = if (is.na(rmse)) NULL else jsonlite::unbox(round(rmse, 4))
  ),
  raster = list(
    width = jsonlite::unbox(ncol(r)),
    height = jsonlite::unbox(nrow(r)),
    data = jsonlite::unbox({
      con <- rawConnection(raw(0), "wb")
      writeBin(as.numeric(filled), con, size = 4, endian = "little")
      b <- rawConnectionValue(con)
      close(con)
      jsonlite::base64_enc(b)
    }),
    wgs84Bounds = round(wgs84_bounds, 6),
    min = jsonlite::unbox(round(min(filled_valid), 4)),
    max = jsonlite::unbox(round(max(filled_valid), 4))
  )
)

jsonlite::fromJSON(jsonlite::toJSON(result_out, null = "null"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

## 6. Why Python takes a different approach here {#why-python-takes-a-different-approach-here}

R's `gstat` (built on `sp`/`sf`) has no WebAssembly build of its
closest Python equivalent, `pykrige`. That's the same gap the
[kriging article](/posts/kriging-soil-sampling.html#why-python-is-reference-only-here)
already documents, and it's true again here for the same reason: no
`pykrige` wheel published for Pyodide. But cokriging specifically has
a second, more interesting wrinkle worth being precise about instead
of glossed over: Python's own [GSTools](https://geostat-framework.readthedocs.io/projects/gstools/en/stable/examples/05_kriging/index.html)
library *does* offer cokriging (Simple and Intrinsic **Collocated**
Cokriging), but that's a genuinely different technique from the
`fit.lmc()` linear model of coregionalization the R cell above fits,
not just a different implementation of the same idea. Collocated
cokriging assumes the covariate is known at every location you're
predicting, and uses that one co-located value directly, without
fitting a full cross-variogram between the two variables the way an
LMC does. It asks less of the data and skips a real modeling step,
which is reasonable when its own assumption holds but not a drop-in
substitute for what this article and the standalone tool actually
compute. No verified reference code for it sits on this page: writing
some without running it against a real GSTools install would risk
teaching a technique this project hasn't actually checked.
